title: Agabus and the belt (Acts 21)
hook: a prophet ties himself with Paul's belt; Paul goes to Jerusalem anyway
carry: the will of the lord be done
tomorrow: a mob, soldiers, a stairway, and he asks to tell a story…

segments.voice: More blessed to give: Paul's goodbye at Miletus, and friends who walked him to the ship. Now the ship lands, and nearly every stop on the way to Jerusalem brings a warning.
screen: `MORE BLESSED TO GIVE.` → `EVERY STOP, A WARNING.`

segments.voice: Pull a belt tight and you feel it at once: the buckle, the pressure, how little room is left. In Caesarea, at the house of Philip the evangelist, a prophet named Agabus walks up to Paul and takes his belt. The King James calls it a girdle. He ties up his own hands and feet with it, right there in the room. Why? So everyone can see, and feel, what's coming.
screen: `THE BUCKLE, THE PRESSURE.` → `AGABUS TAKES THE BELT.` → `HANDS AND FEET, TIED.`

segments.voice: Bound in Paul's belt, Agabus speaks: "Thus saith the Holy Ghost, So shall the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man that owneth this girdle, and shall deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles." This isn't the first warning. In Tyre, disciples told Paul "through the Spirit" not to go up, and when he left anyway, whole families walked him out of town, and "we kneeled down on the shore, and prayed." Knees in the sand, then leather around a prophet's wrists. Now the room breaks: "both we, and they of that place, besought him not to go up to Jerusalem." And Paul answers through their tears: "What mean ye to weep and to break mine heart? for I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus." Here's the one to tell a friend: Paul never calls the prophet wrong. The warning is true, and he goes anyway. In Acts, a warning shows the cost; it doesn't make the choice. Then his friends do something hard. "And when he would not be persuaded, we ceased, saying, The will of the Lord be done." Not a win, not a loss. People who love him, letting go. Paul goes up, and soon a crowd in the temple seizes him, and Roman soldiers take him into custody.
screen: `SO SHALL THEY BIND THE MAN.` · `KNEES ON THE SHORE AT TYRE.` · `READY NOT TO BE BOUND ONLY.` · `WE CEASED.` · then, large: `THE WILL OF THE LORD BE DONE.`

segments.voice: If you're wearing a belt, a watch strap or laced shoes, rest a hand on it and feel how it holds. Bring to mind one place you sense you're meant to go, along with the warnings people have given you. Hold the strap and the warnings together for a moment, eyes open, without deciding anything yet.
Agabus and the belt. A prophet bound with Paul's own belt, a warning Paul heard, and a road he took anyway.
Your line: the will of the Lord be done. His friends said it the moment they stopped arguing. Until tomorrow.

chat.meaning: Paul didn't call Agabus wrong or wave the danger away. He went with eyes open, and his friends said, the will of the Lord be done.

notes: Agabus's words (Acts 21:11) name 'the Jews at Jerusalem' and 'the Gentiles'; quoted exactly from the KJV and not framed against anyone. The teach ends with Roman soldiers taking Paul into custody (Acts 21:31–33). Confirm the framing with a Keeper.
'Soon a crowd in the temple seizes him' paraphrases Acts 21:27–30 (the KJV says 'when the seven days were almost ended'). Confirm.
'Nearly every stop… brings a warning' (review) summarizes Acts 20:23 and 21:4, 11; confirm it isn't overstated.

The index says 'belt'; the KJV says 'girdle'. Both are used. 'Leather around a prophet's wrists' is a sensory picture; Acts doesn't say what the belt was made of. A Keeper may soften to 'a belt around a prophet's wrists'.

'In Acts, a warning shows the cost; it doesn't make the choice' is a reading of 21:10–14. Some readers hear 21:4 ('through the Spirit, that he should not go up') as a stronger prohibition; confirm the framing is fair.
